Chapter 9  ·  Statistical Learning

Gaussian Discriminant Analysis:
Anisotropic Gaussians

From simplified spherical Gaussians to the full multivariate normal — how covariance structure shapes classification geometry

Learning Objectives

  • Interpret the covariance matrix $\Sigma$ geometrically in terms of its eigendecomposition and how it transforms spherical isocontours into ellipsoids.
  • Derive the MLE estimators $\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_c$ and $\hat{\Sigma}_c$ for the class-conditional Gaussian parameters in QDA.
  • Construct and evaluate the quadratic discriminant function $\delta_c(\mathbf{x})$ for multiclass classification.
  • Derive the pooled within-class covariance estimator $\hat{\Sigma}$ used in LDA and explain why within-class means (not the global mean) must be used.
  • Show algebraically that LDA's discriminant function is linear in $\mathbf{x}$ when all classes share a covariance matrix.
  • Compare QDA and LDA in terms of parameter counts, flexibility, overfitting risk, and decision boundary shape.
  • Explain the distinction between the Bayes-optimal classifier (known true parameters) and the fitted QDA/LDA classifiers (estimated parameters).
  • Extend QDA and LDA to accommodate asymmetric loss functions and non-uniform class priors by adjusting the discriminant threshold.

9.1 The Multivariate Normal Distribution: Geometry of Covariance

In Chapter 7 we introduced Gaussian discriminant analysis using a simplified version of the multivariate normal distribution — one in which the covariance was a scalar multiple of the identity, producing spherical, isotropic isocontours. This simplification made the algebra tractable but discarded a key ingredient: the ability to model correlations among features and directional differences in spread. In this chapter we restore the full generality of the covariance matrix $\Sigma$ and revisit how GDA behaves when the Gaussians are truly anisotropic — that is, when they have different widths in different directions and possibly tilted axes.

The central insight, courtesy of the eigendecomposition studied in Chapter 8, is that the covariance matrix $\Sigma$ encodes a complete geometric description of an ellipsoidal shape in feature space. Understanding this geometry is not merely cosmetic; it determines the shape of every decision boundary produced by QDA and LDA, and it governs how well each method generalizes when data are high-dimensional.

We begin by building precise geometric intuition for $\Sigma$ through its eigendecomposition. The key objects are the eigenvectors — which give the principal directions of spread — and the eigenvalues — which give the variance along each such direction. Together they transform an ordinary sphere into the tilted, stretched ellipsoid that characterizes a general multivariate normal distribution.

9.1.1 Eigendecomposition of $\Sigma$ and the Gaussian Widths

Since every valid covariance matrix is real and symmetric, it admits an eigendecomposition of a particularly clean form. Let $\Sigma \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times d}$ be a positive semidefinite matrix. By the spectral theorem, we can write

Definition · Spectral Decomposition of the Covariance Matrix

Let $\Sigma \in \mathbb{R}^{d\times d}$ be a symmetric positive semidefinite matrix. There exist an orthogonal matrix $U = [\mathbf{u}_1 \mid \cdots \mid \mathbf{u}_d]$ whose columns are the eigenvectors of $\Sigma$, and a diagonal matrix $\Gamma = \operatorname{diag}(\gamma_1, \ldots, \gamma_d)$ of non-negative eigenvalues, such that $$\Sigma = U \Gamma U^\top = \sum_{i=1}^{d} \gamma_i \, \mathbf{u}_i \mathbf{u}_i^\top.$$ The eigenvalues $\gamma_i \geq 0$ represent the variance of the distribution along the $i$-th eigenvector direction $\mathbf{u}_i$. The symmetric square root $\Sigma^{1/2} = U \Gamma^{1/2} U^\top$ has eigenvalues $\sqrt{\gamma_i}$, which are the standard deviations — equivalently, the Gaussian widths — along each principal axis.

The matrix $\Sigma^{1/2}$ is particularly important for building geometric intuition. It is the linear map that transforms a unit sphere in $\mathbb{R}^d$ into the ellipsoid that forms the isocontours of the Gaussian. Specifically, if $S_r = \{\mathbf{z} : \|\mathbf{z}\| = r\}$ is the sphere of radius $r$, then $\Sigma^{1/2} S_r = \{\Sigma^{1/2}\mathbf{z} : \|\mathbf{z}\| = r\}$ is an ellipsoid whose semi-axes are $r\sqrt{\gamma_i}$ in the direction $\mathbf{u}_i$. The Gaussian widths $\sigma_i := \sqrt{\gamma_i}$ therefore play the same role as the standard deviation in a univariate normal distribution.

Figure 9.1. Left: isocontours of the quadratic form with $\Sigma = I$ (identity covariance) are perfect circles — all directions have equal variance. Right: isocontours for a general covariance matrix $\Sigma$ with eigenvalues $\gamma_1 > \gamma_2 > 0$ are ellipses aligned with the eigenvectors $\mathbf{u}_1$, $\mathbf{u}_2$ (gold arrows). The semi-axis lengths equal the Gaussian widths $\sigma_i = \sqrt{\gamma_i}$. Notice that the tilt of the ellipses reflects the off-diagonal entries of $\Sigma$ (i.e., the covariance between features). The three nested ellipses correspond to $r = 1, 2, 3$ standard deviations.

9.1.2 The Precision Matrix and the Quadratic Form

The multivariate normal PDF involves not $\Sigma$ but its inverse $\Sigma^{-1}$, called the precision matrix. This matrix appears directly inside the exponent, where it defines the quadratic form that measures the "Mahalanobis distance" from a point $\mathbf{x}$ to the mean $\boldsymbol{\mu}$.

Definition · Precision Matrix and Mahalanobis Distance

Let $\Sigma = U\Gamma U^\top$ be the covariance matrix with eigendecomposition as above, and assume $\Sigma$ is strictly positive definite (all $\gamma_i > 0$). The precision matrix is $\Sigma^{-1} = U \Gamma^{-1} U^\top$, with eigenvalues $1/\gamma_i$ along the same eigenvectors. The squared Mahalanobis distance from $\mathbf{x}$ to $\boldsymbol{\mu}$ is $$q(\mathbf{x}) = (\mathbf{x} - \boldsymbol{\mu})^\top \Sigma^{-1} (\mathbf{x} - \boldsymbol{\mu}) = \sum_{i=1}^{d} \frac{\bigl[(\mathbf{x}-\boldsymbol{\mu})^\top \mathbf{u}_i\bigr]^2}{\gamma_i}.$$ This is a weighted sum of squared projections onto each eigenvector direction, weighted inversely by the variance in that direction.

The precision matrix acts as a metric tensor on feature space: it defines distances by scaling each eigenvector direction inversely by the spread of the distribution in that direction. A high-variance direction (large $\gamma_i$) is shrunk by a factor of $1/\gamma_i$, making large displacements in that direction "cheap." A low-variance direction is penalized heavily, making even small deviations significant. This is precisely the right notion of distance for a Gaussian: a point that is one standard deviation away from the mean in any principal direction has Mahalanobis distance $q(\mathbf{x}) = 1$, regardless of which direction that is.

Intuition · Why Use Mahalanobis Distance?

Euclidean distance treats every direction equally. But if a Gaussian has variance $100$ in the $x_1$ direction and variance $1$ in the $x_2$ direction, being $3$ units away along $x_1$ is much less surprising than being $3$ units away along $x_2$. The Mahalanobis distance corrects for this by normalizing by the standard deviation in each principal direction. Geometrically, it is the Euclidean distance after whitening the data by applying $\Sigma^{-1/2}$: the ellipsoidal isocontours of the Gaussian become spherical isocontours in whitened space, and Euclidean distance in whitened space equals Mahalanobis distance in original space.

9.1.3 From Quadratic Form to Gaussian PDF

With the quadratic form $q(\mathbf{x})$ understood geometrically, the multivariate normal PDF can be written in a decomposed form that separates the geometry from the normalization:

Definition · Multivariate Normal Distribution

A random vector $\mathbf{X} \in \mathbb{R}^d$ follows the multivariate normal distribution $\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{\mu}, \Sigma)$ if its probability density function is $$f(\mathbf{x}) = \frac{1}{(2\pi)^{d/2} |\Sigma|^{1/2}} \exp\!\left(-\frac{1}{2}(\mathbf{x}-\boldsymbol{\mu})^\top \Sigma^{-1}(\mathbf{x}-\boldsymbol{\mu})\right),$$ where $\boldsymbol{\mu} = \mathbb{E}[\mathbf{X}]$ is the mean vector, $\Sigma = \text{Cov}(\mathbf{X})$ is the covariance matrix (symmetric positive definite), and $|\Sigma| = \det(\Sigma) = \prod_{i=1}^d \gamma_i$ is its determinant.

It is helpful to think of the PDF as the composition of two functions: a geometric part $q(\mathbf{x})$ — the quadratic form — and a monotone decreasing transformation $n(t) = (2\pi)^{-d/2}|\Sigma|^{-1/2}\exp(-t/2)$ applied to that quadratic form. The function $n$ is strictly decreasing in $t$, so the isocontours of $f$ (where $f = $ constant) coincide exactly with the isocontours of $q$ (where $q = $ constant). Crucially, this means the shapes of the isocontours are determined entirely by $\Sigma^{-1}$; the normalization factor changes the values assigned to each isocontour but not which points lie on them.

Figure 9.2. Left: the quadratic form $q(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{x}^\top\Sigma^{-1}\mathbf{x}$ for $\Sigma = \begin{pmatrix}2 & 0.8 \\ 0.8 & 0.8\end{pmatrix}$, displayed as a filled contour plot. Three isocontours at $q = 1, 4, 9$ are highlighted. Right: the corresponding Gaussian PDF $\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, \Sigma)$. The isocontour shapes are identical in both panels — the ellipses have the same aspect ratio and orientation — but the values assigned to each isocontour differ because the exponential function rescales the $q$ axis nonlinearly. The key insight is that classification depends only on the isocontour shapes (left panel), not the absolute PDF values.
Example · Computing the Mahalanobis Distance

Setup. Let $d = 2$, $\boldsymbol{\mu} = \mathbf{0}$, and $\Sigma = \begin{pmatrix} 4 & 2 \\ 2 & 2 \end{pmatrix}$. Compute the Mahalanobis distance from the points $\mathbf{a} = (2, 0)^\top$ and $\mathbf{b} = (0, 2)^\top$.

Step 1: Invert $\Sigma$. Using the $2\times 2$ inverse formula, $\det(\Sigma) = 4\cdot 2 - 2\cdot 2 = 4$, so $\Sigma^{-1} = \frac{1}{4}\begin{pmatrix}2 & -2 \\ -2 & 4\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}1/2 & -1/2 \\ -1/2 & 1\end{pmatrix}$.

Step 2: Evaluate $q(\mathbf{a})$. $$q(\mathbf{a}) = (2, 0)\begin{pmatrix}1/2 & -1/2 \\ -1/2 & 1\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}2 \\ 0\end{pmatrix} = (1, -1)\begin{pmatrix}2 \\ 0\end{pmatrix} = 2.$$

Step 3: Evaluate $q(\mathbf{b})$. $$q(\mathbf{b}) = (0, 2)\begin{pmatrix}1/2 & -1/2 \\ -1/2 & 1\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}0 \\ 2\end{pmatrix} = (-1, 2)\begin{pmatrix}0 \\ 2\end{pmatrix} = 4.$$

Result and interpretation. Even though $\|\mathbf{a}\|_2 = \|\mathbf{b}\|_2 = 2$ (both are 2 units from the origin in Euclidean distance), the Mahalanobis distances differ: $\sqrt{q(\mathbf{a})} \approx 1.41$ vs.\ $\sqrt{q(\mathbf{b})} = 2$. Point $\mathbf{b}$ is farther from the mean in the distributional sense because the distribution has less spread in the $x_2$ direction (conditional on $x_1 = 0$, the variance is only $\text{Var}(X_2 | X_1=0) = 2 - 4/4 = 1$).

💡
Key insight: The determinant $|\Sigma| = \prod_i \gamma_i$ in the normalizing constant of the Gaussian PDF equals the product of all eigenvalues. It measures the "volume" of the distribution's spread in all directions simultaneously — it is large when the distribution is spread out (high variance) and small when it is concentrated. This is why the determinant appears in the normalizing constant: a widely spread distribution has lower peak density.

9.2 Maximum Likelihood Estimation for Anisotropic Gaussians

With the geometry of the multivariate normal in hand, we turn to the statistical problem: given a labeled training dataset $\{(\mathbf{x}_i, y_i)\}_{i=1}^n$ where each point $\mathbf{x}_i \in \mathbb{R}^d$ belongs to one of $K$ classes, how do we estimate the parameters of the class-conditional Gaussian $p(\mathbf{x} \mid y = c) = \mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{\mu}_c, \Sigma_c)$? The answer, via maximum likelihood estimation, is both elegant and intuitive.

Two lectures ago we derived MLE estimators for the simplified Gaussian with scalar variance. The principle is identical here — maximize the log-likelihood of the data over all parameters — but the optimization now involves a matrix rather than a scalar. Rather than rederive the full calculation (which, while instructive, is lengthy and would distract from the geometric picture), we state the results and then focus on their interpretation and practical implications.

9.2.1 The MLE Problem for Class-Conditional Gaussians

Let $n_c = |\{i : y_i = c\}|$ denote the number of training points in class $c$. We model each training point $\mathbf{x}_i$ with $y_i = c$ as drawn independently from $\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{\mu}_c, \Sigma_c)$. The log-likelihood for the parameters of class $c$, ignoring constants, is

Class Log-Likelihood
$$\ell_c(\boldsymbol{\mu}_c, \Sigma_c) = -\frac{n_c}{2}\log|\Sigma_c| - \frac{1}{2}\sum_{i:\, y_i = c}(\mathbf{x}_i - \boldsymbol{\mu}_c)^\top \Sigma_c^{-1}(\mathbf{x}_i - \boldsymbol{\mu}_c).$$

Maximizing $\ell_c$ over $\boldsymbol{\mu}_c$ and $\Sigma_c$ jointly yields the estimators given in the next subsection. The full joint log-likelihood over all classes also includes a term for the class priors $\pi_c = P(y = c)$, which are estimated independently from $\boldsymbol{\mu}_c$ and $\Sigma_c$.

9.2.2 MLE Estimators: Means and Covariance Matrices

Theorem · MLE Estimators for Gaussian Discriminant Analysis (QDA)

Given training data $\{(\mathbf{x}_i, y_i)\}_{i=1}^n$ with $\mathbf{x}_i \in \mathbb{R}^d$ and $y_i \in \{1,\ldots,K\}$, the maximum likelihood estimators for the parameters of the class-conditional Gaussian $\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{\mu}_c, \Sigma_c)$ are: $$\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_c = \frac{1}{n_c}\sum_{i:\, y_i = c} \mathbf{x}_i \qquad\text{(sample mean for class }c\text{)},$$ $$\hat{\Sigma}_c = \frac{1}{n_c}\sum_{i:\, y_i = c}(\mathbf{x}_i - \hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_c)(\mathbf{x}_i - \hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_c)^\top \qquad\text{(sample covariance for class }c\text{)},$$ $$\hat{\pi}_c = \frac{n_c}{n} \qquad\text{(estimated class prior)}.$$ These estimators are called the class-conditional sample mean, class-conditional sample covariance, and empirical prior, respectively.

Proof Sketch

For $\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_c$: differentiate $\ell_c$ with respect to $\boldsymbol{\mu}_c$, set to zero. The gradient involves $\sum_{i: y_i=c} \Sigma_c^{-1}(\mathbf{x}_i - \boldsymbol{\mu}_c) = \mathbf{0}$. Since $\Sigma_c^{-1}$ is invertible, this gives $\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_c = n_c^{-1}\sum_{i: y_i=c}\mathbf{x}_i$.

For $\hat{\Sigma}_c$: use the matrix differentiation identities $\partial\log|A|/\partial A = A^{-\top}$ and $\partial \mathbf{a}^\top A^{-1}\mathbf{a}/\partial A = -A^{-\top}\mathbf{a}\mathbf{a}^\top A^{-\top}$. Setting the total derivative of $\ell_c$ with respect to $\Sigma_c^{-1}$ to zero yields $\hat{\Sigma}_c = n_c^{-1}\sum_{i: y_i=c}(\mathbf{x}_i - \hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_c)(\mathbf{x}_i-\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_c)^\top$. □

The formula for $\hat{\Sigma}_c$ has a natural interpretation. Each term $(\mathbf{x}_i - \hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_c)(\mathbf{x}_i - \hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_c)^\top$ is an outer product — a $d \times d$ rank-one matrix that encodes the squared deviation of a single point from the class mean in all directions simultaneously. The diagonal entries are squared deviations in each coordinate; the off-diagonal entries measure correlations. Averaging these rank-one matrices over all $n_c$ class-$c$ points yields a matrix that captures the overall spread and correlation structure of class $c$.

Figure 9.3. MLE fitting with $n = 60$ points per class. Left: QDA — separate covariance matrices $\hat{\Sigma}_C$ (red contours) and $\hat{\Sigma}_D$ (blue contours) are estimated independently. Class means $\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_c$ are shown as crosses. The ellipsoidal contours have different shapes and orientations. Right: LDA — both classes are shown with their QDA contours (solid) alongside the LDA contours (dashed) using the single pooled covariance matrix $\hat{\Sigma}$. The LDA contours are ellipses of identical shape but centered at the two class means, reflecting the shared-covariance assumption.

9.2.3 Positive Definiteness and Singular Sample Covariances

The sample covariance $\hat{\Sigma}_c$ is always positive semidefinite by construction, but it may fail to be strictly positive definite — a requirement for the Gaussian PDF to be well-defined. Specifically, if $n_c \leq d$ (fewer class-$c$ points than dimensions), then the sum of $n_c$ rank-one matrices can have rank at most $n_c < d$, leaving some eigenvalues exactly zero. Even when $n_c > d$, near-collinear features or redundant measurements can produce near-zero eigenvalues, causing numerical difficulties when computing $\hat{\Sigma}_c^{-1}$.

Warning · Singular Sample Covariance in High Dimensions

When the feature dimension $d$ is comparable to or larger than $n_c$, the sample covariance $\hat{\Sigma}_c$ will be singular or near-singular, making direct matrix inversion unreliable. This problem worsens as $d$ grows because $\hat{\Sigma}_c$ has $d(d+1)/2$ free parameters but is estimated from only $n_c$ outer-product matrices. Standard remedies include: (1) regularization, e.g., adding a multiple of the identity $\hat{\Sigma}_c^{\text{reg}} = (1-\alpha)\hat{\Sigma}_c + \alpha I$ (regularized QDA or RDA); (2) dimensionality reduction before fitting; and (3) switching to LDA, which pools class covariances and requires fewer parameters. Choosing $\alpha$ is itself a model selection problem best resolved through cross-validation.

Data Science Application · Covariance Estimation in High-Dimensional Settings

In genomics, a typical dataset might have $d = 20{,}000$ gene expression features and only $n = 200$ samples per class. Here $\hat{\Sigma}_c$ is inevitably singular. Practitioners use shrinkage estimators such as the Ledoit–Wolf estimator, which optimally chooses $\alpha$ in the regularized covariance $\hat{\Sigma}_c^{\text{reg}} = (1-\alpha)\hat{\Sigma}_c + \alpha I$ to minimize mean squared error to the true $\Sigma_c$. Alternatively, diagonal LDA (sometimes called "naive Bayes" for continuous features) sets all off-diagonal entries to zero, dramatically reducing the parameter count to $d$ per class at the cost of ignoring inter-feature correlations. Despite this crude approximation, diagonal LDA often performs competitively on gene expression data because the signal-to-noise ratio is low and off-diagonal entries are poorly estimated.

9.3 Quadratic Discriminant Analysis (QDA)

With the MLE estimators in hand, we now describe the complete QDA classification procedure. The strategy, inherited from our general treatment of Bayesian classification in Chapter 7, is to assign a test point $\mathbf{x}$ to the class that maximizes the posterior probability $P(y = c \mid \mathbf{x})$. By Bayes' theorem, this is equivalent to maximizing the product of the class-conditional density and the prior: $p(\mathbf{x} \mid y = c) \cdot P(y = c)$. Taking logarithms — which preserve the argmax — and dropping constants that do not depend on $c$, we arrive at the quadratic discriminant function.

The "quadratic" in QDA refers to the shape of this discriminant function as a function of the test point $\mathbf{x}$: because each class has its own covariance matrix $\Sigma_c$, the quadratic form $(\mathbf{x}-\boldsymbol{\mu}_c)^\top\Sigma_c^{-1}(\mathbf{x}-\boldsymbol{\mu}_c)$ remains quadratic in $\mathbf{x}$, and no cancellation occurs across classes. This is in contrast to LDA, treated in Section 9.4, where identical covariance matrices cause the quadratic terms to cancel.

9.3.1 The Quadratic Discriminant Function

Definition · Quadratic Discriminant Function

Under the model $p(\mathbf{x} \mid y = c) = \mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{\mu}_c, \Sigma_c)$ with prior $P(y = c) = \pi_c$, the quadratic discriminant function for class $c$ is $$\delta_c(\mathbf{x}) = -\frac{1}{2}\log|\Sigma_c| - \frac{1}{2}(\mathbf{x}-\boldsymbol{\mu}_c)^\top\Sigma_c^{-1}(\mathbf{x}-\boldsymbol{\mu}_c) + \log\pi_c.$$ The QDA classifier assigns $\mathbf{x}$ to the class $\hat{c}(\mathbf{x}) = \operatorname*{arg\,max}_{c \in \{1,\ldots,K\}} \delta_c(\mathbf{x})$.

Each term in $\delta_c$ has a clear role. The term $-\frac{1}{2}\log|\Sigma_c|$ penalizes classes with large covariance matrices: a spread-out Gaussian has lower peak density, and this term reflects that penalty. The term $-\frac{1}{2}(\mathbf{x}-\boldsymbol{\mu}_c)^\top\Sigma_c^{-1}(\mathbf{x}-\boldsymbol{\mu}_c)$ is the (negative) squared Mahalanobis distance from $\mathbf{x}$ to class $c$'s mean, measuring how surprising $\mathbf{x}$ is under class $c$'s distribution. The term $\log\pi_c$ incorporates the prior: classes that are intrinsically more common receive a boost.

QDA Classification Rule
$$\hat{c}(\mathbf{x}) = \operatorname*{arg\,max}_{c} \left[-\frac{1}{2}\log|\hat{\Sigma}_c| - \frac{1}{2}(\mathbf{x}-\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_c)^\top\hat{\Sigma}_c^{-1}(\mathbf{x}-\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_c) + \log\hat{\pi}_c\right]$$

9.3.2 Decision Boundaries as Quadric Surfaces

The QDA decision boundary between classes $c$ and $d$ is the set of points where $\delta_c(\mathbf{x}) = \delta_d(\mathbf{x})$, i.e., where neither class is preferred over the other. Setting $\delta_c(\mathbf{x}) - \delta_d(\mathbf{x}) = 0$ and expanding, we see that this equation involves terms up to degree two in $\mathbf{x}$ — specifically $\mathbf{x}^\top(\Sigma_c^{-1} - \Sigma_d^{-1})\mathbf{x}$. In two dimensions these curves are conic sections (ellipses, hyperbolas, or parabolas); in $d$ dimensions they are quadric hypersurfaces. This rich family of boundary shapes is what gives QDA its flexibility.

Example · QDA Decision Function for Two Gaussians

Setup. Consider two classes with parameters $\boldsymbol{\mu}_C = (-1, 1)^\top$, $\boldsymbol{\mu}_D = (1, -1)^\top$, $\Sigma_C = \begin{pmatrix}2 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{pmatrix}$, $\Sigma_D = \begin{pmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{pmatrix}$, and equal priors $\pi_C = \pi_D = 0.5$.

Discriminant difference. The decision function is $\delta_C(\mathbf{x}) - \delta_D(\mathbf{x})$. Since $\pi_C = \pi_D$ the log-prior terms cancel. We compute $\det(\Sigma_C) = 2\cdot1 - 1\cdot1 = 1$ and $\det(\Sigma_D) = 2$, so the log-determinant term contributes $-\frac{1}{2}\log 1 + \frac{1}{2}\log 2 = \frac{\log 2}{2} \approx 0.347$ in favor of class $D$.

Quadratic coefficient. The difference of the precision matrices $\Sigma_C^{-1} - \Sigma_D^{-1}$ has both zero and nonzero off-diagonal entries, producing a genuinely quadratic (not merely linear) expression in $\mathbf{x}$. The decision boundary $\delta_C = \delta_D$ is therefore a conic section — in this case an ellipse or hyperbola — rather than a straight line.

Interpretation. The asymmetry between $\Sigma_C$ (high covariance, aligned diagonally) and $\Sigma_D$ (axis-aligned, different aspect ratio) produces a curved decision boundary. Near the origin, where both Gaussians have moderate density, the precise shape of the boundary is determined by the difference of their quadratic forms — something that LDA cannot capture because LDA forces this difference to be zero.

9.3.3 Posterior Probabilities and the Logistic Connection

Beyond classifying a point, we often want to know how confident the classifier is. In the two-class case, the posterior probability that $\mathbf{x}$ belongs to class $C$ is

$$P(y = C \mid \mathbf{x}) = \frac{\pi_C \, p(\mathbf{x} \mid C)}{\pi_C \, p(\mathbf{x} \mid C) + \pi_D \, p(\mathbf{x} \mid D)} = \frac{1}{1 + \exp(-(\delta_C(\mathbf{x}) - \delta_D(\mathbf{x})))}.$$

This is the logistic (sigmoid) function applied to the discriminant difference $\delta_C - \delta_D$. Since $\delta_C - \delta_D$ is a quadratic function of $\mathbf{x}$, the posterior probability is the logistic function of a quadratic — a generalized logistic regression with quadratic features. The decision boundary ($P = 0.5$) is where $\delta_C = \delta_D$; the gradient of the posterior is steepest at this boundary and flattens as we move far into either class's region.

Figure 9.4. QDA classification pipeline for two anisotropic Gaussian classes. Left: class PDFs with isocontours in red (class C) and blue (class D); the gold curve is the decision boundary where $\delta_C = \delta_D$. Center: the discriminant difference $\delta_C(\mathbf{x}) - \delta_D(\mathbf{x})$ — red regions favor class C, blue favor class D; the gold contour is the zero isocontour (decision boundary). Right: posterior probability $P(C \mid \mathbf{x})$ obtained by applying the logistic function to the discriminant difference. The steepest transition occurs at the gold 50% contour (decision boundary). Notice how the curved decision boundary captures the asymmetric spread of the two Gaussians.

The multiclass case extends naturally. For $K > 2$ classes, one computes $\delta_c(\mathbf{x})$ for each class and assigns to the winner. There is no single "decision function" — instead, there is a family of $K$ quadratic bowls, and classification returns the index of the highest bowl at the query point, as illustrated in Section 9.5.

9.4 Linear Discriminant Analysis (LDA)

Linear discriminant analysis (LDA) is the special case of Gaussian discriminant analysis in which we assume all classes share the same covariance matrix: $\Sigma_c = \Sigma$ for all $c$. This constraint is imposed not because we believe it is literally true, but because it dramatically reduces the number of parameters we need to estimate, lowering overfitting risk at the cost of some model flexibility. When the true covariance matrices are indeed similar across classes, LDA can outperform QDA despite its less flexible decision boundaries — the data is simply insufficient to reliably estimate the additional parameters that QDA requires.

The key algebraic miracle of LDA is that when all classes share a covariance matrix, the quadratic terms in the discriminant function $\delta_c(\mathbf{x}) - \delta_d(\mathbf{x})$ cancel exactly, leaving a decision function that is linear in $\mathbf{x}$. This is not an approximation — it is an exact algebraic identity. The result is a hyperplane decision boundary, regardless of how complex the Gaussian distributions themselves may look.

9.4.1 The Pooled Within-Class Covariance Matrix

To implement LDA we need a single covariance estimate $\hat{\Sigma}$ that reflects the within-class spread for all classes simultaneously. The natural choice is a weighted average of the class-conditional sample covariances, where the weights are the class sizes.

Definition · Pooled Within-Class Covariance Matrix

Given class-conditional sample covariances $\hat{\Sigma}_c$ for $c = 1, \ldots, K$ with $n_c$ points in class $c$, the pooled within-class covariance matrix is $$\hat{\Sigma} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{c=1}^K \sum_{i:\,y_i = c}(\mathbf{x}_i - \hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_c)(\mathbf{x}_i - \hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_c)^\top = \sum_{c=1}^{K} \frac{n_c}{n}\,\hat{\Sigma}_c.$$ It is critical that each deviation is computed from the class mean $\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_c$, not the global mean $\bar{\mathbf{x}} = n^{-1}\sum_i \mathbf{x}_i$. Using the global mean would conflate within-class spread with between-class spread, producing an inflated covariance estimate that is inappropriate for classification.

Warning · Always Use Class Means, Not the Global Mean

A common implementation error is to compute the pooled covariance as $\frac{1}{n}\sum_i (\mathbf{x}_i - \bar{\mathbf{x}})(\mathbf{x}_i - \bar{\mathbf{x}})^\top$ using the global mean $\bar{\mathbf{x}}$. This is the total sample covariance, which decomposes as $\hat{\Sigma}_{\text{total}} = \hat{\Sigma}_{\text{within}} + \hat{\Sigma}_{\text{between}}$, where $\hat{\Sigma}_{\text{between}} = \sum_c \frac{n_c}{n}(\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_c - \bar{\mathbf{x}})(\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_c-\bar{\mathbf{x}})^\top$ measures between-class spread. LDA requires $\hat{\Sigma}_{\text{within}}$ — the within-class covariance — not the total covariance. The between-class term can be substantial whenever classes are well-separated, inflating $\hat{\Sigma}$ and leading to an overly conservative (less discriminative) classifier.

9.4.2 Cancellation of Quadratic Terms and the Linear Classifier

With a shared covariance $\Sigma$, the discriminant function for class $c$ becomes $\delta_c(\mathbf{x}) = -\frac{1}{2}\log|\Sigma| - \frac{1}{2}(\mathbf{x}-\boldsymbol{\mu}_c)^\top\Sigma^{-1}(\mathbf{x}-\boldsymbol{\mu}_c) + \log\pi_c$. The log-determinant term $-\frac{1}{2}\log|\Sigma|$ is now the same for all classes and drops out of any discriminant difference. The quadratic term in $\mathbf{x}$ also cancels.

Theorem · LDA Produces a Linear Decision Boundary

When all classes share the covariance matrix $\Sigma$, the discriminant difference between classes $c$ and $d$ is linear in $\mathbf{x}$: $$\delta_c(\mathbf{x}) - \delta_d(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{w}^\top \mathbf{x} + \alpha_{cd},$$ where $$\mathbf{w} = \Sigma^{-1}(\boldsymbol{\mu}_c - \boldsymbol{\mu}_d), \qquad \alpha_{cd} = -\frac{1}{2}\boldsymbol{\mu}_c^\top\Sigma^{-1}\boldsymbol{\mu}_c + \frac{1}{2}\boldsymbol{\mu}_d^\top\Sigma^{-1}\boldsymbol{\mu}_d + \log\frac{\pi_c}{\pi_d}.$$ The LDA decision boundary between classes $c$ and $d$ is the hyperplane $\{\mathbf{x}: \mathbf{w}^\top\mathbf{x} + \alpha_{cd} = 0\}$.

Proof

Expand the quadratic forms in $\delta_c$ and $\delta_d$ using the identity $(\mathbf{x}-\boldsymbol{\mu})^\top A(\mathbf{x}-\boldsymbol{\mu}) = \mathbf{x}^\top A\mathbf{x} - 2\boldsymbol{\mu}^\top A\mathbf{x} + \boldsymbol{\mu}^\top A\boldsymbol{\mu}$: $$\delta_c - \delta_d = \underbrace{\left(-\tfrac{1}{2}\mathbf{x}^\top\Sigma^{-1}\mathbf{x} + \boldsymbol{\mu}_c^\top\Sigma^{-1}\mathbf{x} - \tfrac{1}{2}\boldsymbol{\mu}_c^\top\Sigma^{-1}\boldsymbol{\mu}_c\right)}_{\delta_c(\mathbf{x}), \text{ quadratic part}} - \underbrace{\left(-\tfrac{1}{2}\mathbf{x}^\top\Sigma^{-1}\mathbf{x} + \boldsymbol{\mu}_d^\top\Sigma^{-1}\mathbf{x} - \tfrac{1}{2}\boldsymbol{\mu}_d^\top\Sigma^{-1}\boldsymbol{\mu}_d\right)}_{\delta_d(\mathbf{x}), \text{ quadratic part}} + \log\tfrac{\pi_c}{\pi_d}.$$ The terms $-\frac{1}{2}\mathbf{x}^\top\Sigma^{-1}\mathbf{x}$ cancel, leaving $(\boldsymbol{\mu}_c - \boldsymbol{\mu}_d)^\top\Sigma^{-1}\mathbf{x} + \text{constants}$. Setting $\mathbf{w} = \Sigma^{-1}(\boldsymbol{\mu}_c-\boldsymbol{\mu}_d)$ and collecting constant terms into $\alpha_{cd}$ yields the stated result. □

LDA Discriminant (Pairwise)
$$\delta_c(\mathbf{x}) - \delta_d(\mathbf{x}) = (\boldsymbol{\mu}_c - \boldsymbol{\mu}_d)^\top \Sigma^{-1}\mathbf{x} - \frac{1}{2}(\boldsymbol{\mu}_c^\top\Sigma^{-1}\boldsymbol{\mu}_c - \boldsymbol{\mu}_d^\top\Sigma^{-1}\boldsymbol{\mu}_d) + \log\frac{\pi_c}{\pi_d}$$
Figure 9.5. LDA classification pipeline. Left: the two classes share a covariance matrix $\Sigma = \begin{pmatrix}1.5 & 0.9 \\ 0.9 & 1.2\end{pmatrix}$, so their isocontours have identical shapes but are centered at different means. The gold line is the linear decision boundary. Center: the discriminant difference $\delta_C - \delta_D$ is a perfectly planar function of $\mathbf{x}$ — its isocontours are straight parallel lines. Right: posterior probability $P(C \mid \mathbf{x})$ from the logistic function applied to the linear discriminant. The transition from 0 to 1 is symmetric around the gold 50% boundary, reflecting the linear structure.

9.4.3 Multiclass LDA via Per-Class Linear Discriminants

For $K > 2$ classes, we do not need to compute a pairwise discriminant for every pair — that would require $\binom{K}{2}$ computations per test point. Instead, we define a linear discriminant function for each class independently, computed from the terms that depend only on class $c$, and assign the test point to the class with the highest value.

Definition · Per-Class Linear Discriminant (LDA, Multiclass)

Under the shared covariance assumption, the per-class linear discriminant function is $$\tilde{\delta}_c(\mathbf{x}) = \boldsymbol{\mu}_c^\top \Sigma^{-1} \mathbf{x} - \frac{1}{2}\boldsymbol{\mu}_c^\top\Sigma^{-1}\boldsymbol{\mu}_c + \log\pi_c.$$ The multiclass LDA rule is $\hat{c}(\mathbf{x}) = \operatorname*{arg\,max}_{c} \tilde{\delta}_c(\mathbf{x})$. The vector $\mathbf{w}_c = \Sigma^{-1}\boldsymbol{\mu}_c$ should be precomputed once and reused — it solves the linear system $\Sigma \mathbf{w}_c = \boldsymbol{\mu}_c$.

Note that $\tilde{\delta}_c(\mathbf{x}) - \tilde{\delta}_d(\mathbf{x}) = \delta_c(\mathbf{x}) - \delta_d(\mathbf{x})$ as defined in the theorem above, so the pairwise comparison is equivalent. The per-class formulation is simply more efficient for large $K$: we compute $K$ values rather than $\binom{K}{2}$ pairwise differences.

⚙️
Implementation note: The vector $\mathbf{w}_c = \Sigma^{-1}\boldsymbol{\mu}_c$ appears in the classification rule for every test point. Do not compute $\Sigma^{-1}$ explicitly (numerically unstable) — instead solve the linear system $\Sigma \mathbf{w}_c = \boldsymbol{\mu}_c$ once per class using a Cholesky factorization (since $\Sigma$ is symmetric positive definite). Store the $K$ vectors $\mathbf{w}_c$ and reuse them for every test point. This reduces the per-point classification cost from $O(d^2)$ to $O(Kd)$ — a huge saving when $d$ is large.
Figure 9.7. Multiclass QDA applied to 10 classes in two dimensions. Each colored region is the set of test points assigned to that class. The black curves are the quadratic decision boundaries — conic sections arising from the equality $\delta_c(\mathbf{x}) = \delta_d(\mathbf{x})$ for adjacent classes $c, d$. Stars mark class means; dots are training samples. The complex, irregular tessellation of the plane reflects the differing covariance matrices of the 10 classes. For LDA (shared covariance), all decision boundaries would be straight lines, producing a simpler Voronoi-like tessellation.

9.5 Comparing QDA and LDA

Having derived both QDA and LDA from first principles, we are now in a position to compare them systematically. The comparison involves at least three dimensions: parameter count (and hence overfitting risk), the nature of achievable decision boundaries, and the relationship between the fitted classifiers and the theoretically optimal Bayes classifier. Understanding when each method is appropriate requires engaging with all three dimensions.

It is tempting to say "QDA is always better because it is more general." This ignores the fundamental bias-variance tradeoff: a more flexible model requires more data to fit reliably, and in finite samples, the variance introduced by fitting extra parameters can overwhelm the bias reduction. The right choice between QDA and LDA is a data-dependent question, best answered by cross-validation.

9.5.1 Parameter Counts and the Bias-Variance Tradeoff

Theorem · Parameter Counts for LDA and QDA

For a $K$-class problem in $\mathbb{R}^d$, the total number of free parameters learned by each method is:

  • LDA: $K \cdot d$ (class means) $+ \, d(d+1)/2$ (one shared covariance) $+ \, (K-1)$ (class priors) $= O(Kd + d^2)$. The effective dimension of the decision surface is $d + 1$ (one weight vector and one bias for each pairwise boundary, but the boundaries are not independent).
  • QDA: $K \cdot d$ (class means) $+ \, K \cdot d(d+1)/2$ (one covariance per class) $+ \, (K-1)$ (class priors) $= O(Kd^2)$.
As $d$ grows, QDA's parameter count grows as $O(Kd^2)$ while LDA's grows as $O(Kd + d^2)$. The quadratic growth of QDA's parameter count makes it increasingly vulnerable to overfitting in high-dimensional settings.

Figure 9.8. Total parameter count for LDA (blue) and QDA (red) as the feature dimension $d$ grows from 1 to 50, with $K = 5$ classes. LDA's effective parameter count grows approximately linearly in $d$, while QDA's grows quadratically (note the log scale on the $y$-axis). At $d = 50$, QDA has approximately $5 \times 50 \times 51 / 2 \approx 6{,}375$ covariance parameters alone, compared to LDA's single $50 \times 50 / 2 = 1{,}275$-parameter covariance. Each additional feature dimension adds $5 \times d$ new covariance parameters to QDA but only $d$ to LDA.

9.5.2 Bayes Optimality vs. Fitted Classifiers

There are two distinct uses of the QDA/LDA discriminant functions, and conflating them is a common source of confusion. The first use is as a Bayes-optimal classifier: if the true data-generating distribution is exactly $p(\mathbf{x} \mid y = c) = \mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{\mu}_c, \Sigma_c)$ for known $\boldsymbol{\mu}_c, \Sigma_c, \pi_c$, then the QDA rule achieves the minimum possible classification error (Bayes error) over all classifiers. In this scenario, the decision boundaries drawn using the true parameters are the "purple lines" shown in many textbook figures. The second use is as a data-driven classifier: in the real world, we substitute $\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_c, \hat{\Sigma}_c, \hat{\pi}_c$ for the unknown true parameters. This is QDA as a learning algorithm, and it no longer guarantees Bayes optimality.

Intuition · Why the Bayes Classifier Doesn't Exist in the Real World

The Bayes-optimal classifier requires knowing the exact true distributions. With real data we face two fundamental limitations: (1) we can only estimate the parameters from finitely many samples, introducing estimation error; and (2) real-world data almost never comes from exactly Gaussian distributions. Even if we had infinite data, the Gaussian assumption might be violated. The textbook "Bayes boundary" figures are possible only because the data is computer-generated from a known distribution. In practice, both QDA and LDA should be viewed as approximations that happen to work well when the Gaussian assumption is roughly satisfied and the sample size is adequate relative to the parameter count.

The practical implication: when reading research papers or textbook comparisons, always check whether the reported boundaries are Bayes-optimal (computed from true parameters) or fitted (computed from data). The former tells you about the ideal we are approximating; the latter tells you how well a real learning algorithm performs.

Figure 9.6. Comparison of QDA (teal, dash-dot) and LDA (green, dotted) against the true Bayes-optimal boundary (purple, dashed) in two scenarios, with $n = 80$ points per class. Left (Scenario A): the true boundary is linear (both classes have identical covariances), so LDA fits well and QDA overfits — QDA's extra flexibility is wasted, and its decision boundary wiggles unnecessarily. Right (Scenario B): the classes have very different covariance shapes ($\Sigma_C$ is tall and narrow, $\Sigma_D$ is wide and flat), making the true boundary curved. LDA is forced to use a straight line and therefore underfits; QDA correctly captures the curved boundary. This illustrates that neither method dominates universally — the right choice depends on the data.

9.5.3 Adjusting for Asymmetric Loss and Non-Uniform Priors

Our derivation assumed a symmetric $0$-$1$ loss (all misclassifications are equally bad) and classified at the 50% posterior threshold. Both assumptions can be relaxed. Suppose we have an asymmetric loss matrix: a false positive (predicting class $C$ when truth is $D$) costs $\lambda_{FP}$ and a false negative costs $\lambda_{FN}$. The optimal Bayes rule minimizes expected loss, which shifts the threshold away from 50%.

Theorem · Classification Threshold Under Asymmetric Loss

Under asymmetric costs $(\lambda_{FP}, \lambda_{FN})$ with equal priors, the optimal decision rule classifies $\mathbf{x}$ as class $C$ if and only if $$P(C \mid \mathbf{x}) > \frac{\lambda_{FP}}{\lambda_{FP} + \lambda_{FN}} =: p^*.$$ In terms of the discriminant, this is equivalent to $\delta_C(\mathbf{x}) - \delta_D(\mathbf{x}) > \log\frac{p^*}{1-p^*}$. For asymmetric priors $\pi_C \neq \pi_D$, the log-prior term $\log(\pi_C/\pi_D)$ absorbs this adjustment, and the threshold on the discriminant becomes $\delta_C - \delta_D > \log\frac{p^*}{1-p^*} - \log\frac{\pi_C}{\pi_D}$.

Geometrically, changing $p^*$ from 0.5 is equivalent to shifting the decision boundary in the feature space. In the posterior probability picture (right panel of Figure 9.4 and 9.5), one simply moves from the 50% isocontour to the $p^*$ isocontour. This is computationally free — the same discriminant functions are used, only the threshold changes. The framework thus provides a complete, principled approach to cost-sensitive classification without any modification to the training procedure.

Data Science Application · Medical Diagnosis and Asymmetric Loss

In medical screening, a false negative (missing a disease) is typically far more costly than a false positive (unnecessary follow-up testing). If $\lambda_{FN} = 10\lambda_{FP}$ — missing disease is 10 times worse than a false alarm — then $p^* = \lambda_{FP}/(\lambda_{FP}+\lambda_{FN}) = 1/11 \approx 9.1\%$. The classifier should flag any patient as positive if the posterior probability exceeds 9.1%, dramatically increasing sensitivity at the cost of specificity. With Gaussian discriminant models, this threshold shift is achieved simply by modifying the cutoff on $\delta_C - \delta_D$; no retraining is required. This flexibility — the ability to tune the operating point of the classifier post-hoc — is one of the practical advantages of probabilistic classifiers like LDA and QDA over non-probabilistic methods such as SVMs.

A final practical note: the StatLog project, which evaluated dozens of classifiers on 22 benchmark datasets spanning domains from satellite imagery to medical records, found that one of LDA or QDA ranked in the top three classifiers for over 10 of the 22 datasets. These methods are competitive not because real-world data is Gaussian — it usually is not — but because Gaussian models yield stable covariance estimates that generalize well when the true decision boundary is roughly linear or quadratic. As with any machine learning algorithm, validation on held-out data is the ultimate arbiter of which method to use.

✦ Chapter Summary

This chapter developed the full, anisotropic version of Gaussian discriminant analysis. The covariance matrix $\Sigma$ encodes a complete geometric description of a multivariate Gaussian through its eigendecomposition: the eigenvectors give the principal directions of spread, and the eigenvalues $\gamma_i$ give the variance along each direction, with the Gaussian widths being $\sigma_i = \sqrt{\gamma_i}$. The precision matrix $\Sigma^{-1}$ appears in the Gaussian PDF as a metric tensor defining the Mahalanobis distance — the correct notion of distance for a Gaussian-distributed population. MLE produces the sample mean and sample covariance as the natural estimators for each class. QDA uses these estimates directly, yielding quadratic discriminant functions and quadric decision boundaries. LDA imposes the constraint of a shared pooled covariance, causing quadratic terms to cancel exactly and producing hyperplane boundaries — linear classifiers with a rigorous probabilistic foundation. The two methods represent different points on the bias-variance tradeoff: LDA is more constrained but estimates fewer parameters; QDA is more flexible but requires more data. Neither dominates universally, and validation is essential for choosing between them in practice.

COVARIANCE EIGENDECOMPOSITION

The spectral decomposition $\Sigma = U\Gamma U^\top$ reveals the principal directions (eigenvectors $\mathbf{u}_i$) and variances (eigenvalues $\gamma_i$) of a Gaussian. The symmetric square root $\Sigma^{1/2}$ maps unit spheres to isocontour ellipsoids with semi-axis lengths $\sigma_i = \sqrt{\gamma_i}$ (Gaussian widths). The inverse $\Sigma^{-1}$ is the precision matrix with the same eigenvectors but inverted eigenvalues.

MAHALANOBIS DISTANCE

The quadratic form $q(\mathbf{x}) = (\mathbf{x}-\boldsymbol{\mu})^\top\Sigma^{-1}(\mathbf{x}-\boldsymbol{\mu})$ is the squared Mahalanobis distance. It normalizes deviations by the distributional variance in each principal direction: $q(\mathbf{x}) = \sum_i [(\mathbf{x}-\boldsymbol{\mu})^\top\mathbf{u}_i]^2/\gamma_i$. The isocontours $q = r^2$ are ellipsoids — the isocontours of the Gaussian PDF.

MLE ESTIMATORS

Maximum likelihood yields $\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_c = n_c^{-1}\sum_{i:y_i=c}\mathbf{x}_i$ (class sample mean) and $\hat{\Sigma}_c = n_c^{-1}\sum_{i:y_i=c}(\mathbf{x}_i-\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_c)(\mathbf{x}_i-\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_c)^\top$ (class sample covariance, a sum of rank-one outer products). The estimated prior is $\hat{\pi}_c = n_c/n$. These estimators are consistent and efficient for Gaussian data.

QDA DISCRIMINANT

The quadratic discriminant function $\delta_c(\mathbf{x}) = -\frac{1}{2}\log|\Sigma_c| - \frac{1}{2}(\mathbf{x}-\boldsymbol{\mu}_c)^\top\Sigma_c^{-1}(\mathbf{x}-\boldsymbol{\mu}_c) + \log\pi_c$ combines the log-determinant penalty (spread), the Mahalanobis distance (fit), and the log-prior. Classification: $\hat{c}(\mathbf{x}) = \operatorname*{arg\,max}_c \delta_c(\mathbf{x})$.

QUADRIC DECISION BOUNDARIES

QDA boundaries between classes $c$ and $d$ are zero-sets of the quadratic function $\delta_c - \delta_d$, involving $\mathbf{x}^\top(\Sigma_c^{-1}-\Sigma_d^{-1})\mathbf{x}$. In $\mathbb{R}^2$ these are conic sections; in $\mathbb{R}^d$ they are quadric hypersurfaces. In two classes, the posterior is the logistic function applied to the quadratic $\delta_C - \delta_D$.

POOLED COVARIANCE (LDA)

The pooled within-class covariance $\hat{\Sigma} = n^{-1}\sum_c\sum_{i:y_i=c}(\mathbf{x}_i-\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_c)(\mathbf{x}_i-\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_c)^\top = \sum_c \frac{n_c}{n}\hat{\Sigma}_c$ uses class means — never the global mean. It is the weighted average of the class-conditional covariances and serves as LDA's single shared covariance estimate.

LDA LINEARITY THEOREM

When all classes share $\Sigma$, the quadratic terms $\mathbf{x}^\top\Sigma^{-1}\mathbf{x}$ cancel in $\delta_c - \delta_d$, leaving the purely linear classifier $\delta_c - \delta_d = (\boldsymbol{\mu}_c-\boldsymbol{\mu}_d)^\top\Sigma^{-1}\mathbf{x} + \alpha_{cd}$. This algebraic cancellation is exact and is the defining property of LDA: it forces hyperplane boundaries regardless of the Gaussian shapes.

PARAMETER COUNTS

LDA has $O(Kd+d^2)$ parameters — the shared covariance dominates at $d(d+1)/2$. QDA has $O(Kd^2)$ — one covariance per class, each with $d(d+1)/2$ entries. As $d$ grows, QDA's parameter count blows up quadratically, making it increasingly prone to overfitting when $n$ is fixed. LDA is preferred when $n/d$ is small.

BAYES VS. FITTED CLASSIFIER

With true parameters plugged in, QDA achieves Bayes-optimal error if data are truly Gaussian. With estimated $\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_c, \hat{\Sigma}_c, \hat{\pi}_c$, QDA/LDA are data-driven approximations. Real data is rarely exactly Gaussian; the "Bayes boundary" (purple curves in textbooks) is available only for computer-generated data from known distributions.

ASYMMETRIC LOSS

Under loss $\lambda_{FP}$ for false positives and $\lambda_{FN}$ for false negatives, classify as positive if $P(C|\mathbf{x}) > p^* = \lambda_{FP}/(\lambda_{FP}+\lambda_{FN})$. This is equivalent to shifting the discriminant threshold from 0 to $\log(p^*/(1-p^*))$. No retraining is needed — only the decision threshold changes, enabling post-hoc calibration to the cost structure.

Exercises

Exercise 9.1 · Eigendecomposition and Gaussian Geometry
Characterizing Ellipsoidal Isocontours in Satellite Image Feature Spaces

Consider a covariance matrix $\Sigma = \begin{pmatrix}5 & 3 \\ 3 & 2\end{pmatrix}$ used to model feature distributions in a satellite image classification task.

  1. (a) Derivation: Compute the eigenvalues $\gamma_1 \geq \gamma_2 > 0$ and the corresponding unit eigenvectors $\mathbf{u}_1, \mathbf{u}_2$ of $\Sigma$. Verify that your eigenvectors are orthogonal. What are the Gaussian widths $\sigma_1, \sigma_2$?
  2. (b) Computation: Write down the precision matrix $\Sigma^{-1}$ explicitly. Compute the Mahalanobis distance from the origin to the point $\mathbf{p} = (2, -1)^\top$. Compare this to the Euclidean distance $\|\mathbf{p}\|_2$ and explain why they differ.
  3. (c) Interpretation: Describe the isocontour $\{\mathbf{x}: (\mathbf{x}-\boldsymbol{\mu})^\top\Sigma^{-1}(\mathbf{x}-\boldsymbol{\mu}) = 4\}$ geometrically (center, semi-axis lengths, and orientation) for $\boldsymbol{\mu} = (1, 1)^\top$.
  4. (d) Extension: In satellite image classification with $d = 200$ spectral bands, computing $\Sigma^{-1}$ exactly may be ill-conditioned. Propose a regularized precision matrix $\Sigma_{\lambda}^{-1}$ and explain how the Mahalanobis isocontours change as the regularization parameter $\lambda$ increases from 0 to $\infty$.
Exercise 9.2 · MLE for Class-Conditional Gaussians
Fitting Gaussian Models to Handwritten Digit Feature Distributions

You are building a digit classifier using two features: average pixel intensity $x_1$ and stroke length variance $x_2$. For digit class "$0$" you observe $n_0 = 4$ training points: $(2, 3), (3, 4), (2, 5), (3, 2)$. For digit class "$1$" you observe $n_1 = 3$ training points: $(6, 1), (7, 2), (6, 0)$.

  1. (a) Derivation: Starting from the log-likelihood expression $\ell_c(\boldsymbol{\mu}_c, \Sigma_c) = -\frac{n_c}{2}\log|\Sigma_c| - \frac{1}{2}\sum_{i:y_i=c}(\mathbf{x}_i-\boldsymbol{\mu}_c)^\top\Sigma_c^{-1}(\mathbf{x}_i-\boldsymbol{\mu}_c)$, compute $\partial\ell_c/\partial\boldsymbol{\mu}_c$ and show it yields the sample mean formula.
  2. (b) Computation: Compute $\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_0$, $\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_1$, $\hat{\Sigma}_0$, $\hat{\Sigma}_1$, and $\hat{\pi}_0$, $\hat{\pi}_1$ explicitly. Verify that both sample covariance matrices are positive semidefinite.
  3. (c) Interpretation: Is $\hat{\Sigma}_0$ or $\hat{\Sigma}_1$ positive definite (not just semidefinite)? If not, explain why, and describe one practical remedy.
  4. (d) Data Science Application: For a test point $\mathbf{z} = (4, 2)^\top$, compute $\delta_0(\mathbf{z})$ and $\delta_1(\mathbf{z})$ using the QDA rule (handling any singularity as you see fit) and state the predicted class.
Exercise 9.3 · From QDA to LDA: The Cancellation Argument
Proving and Visualizing the Linearity of LDA in Medical Imaging Classification

Consider three classes (healthy tissue, benign tumor, malignant tumor) in a $d$-dimensional imaging feature space. All three classes share a covariance matrix $\Sigma$ (LDA assumption).

  1. (a) Derivation: Prove in detail that the discriminant difference $\delta_c(\mathbf{x}) - \delta_d(\mathbf{x})$ is linear in $\mathbf{x}$ for any two classes $c, d$ under the shared-covariance assumption. Your proof should identify precisely which terms cancel and why.
  2. (b) Computation: For $d = 2$, $\boldsymbol{\mu}_1 = (0,0)^\top$, $\boldsymbol{\mu}_2 = (3,1)^\top$, $\Sigma = \begin{pmatrix}2 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{pmatrix}$, and equal priors, find the explicit equation $w_1 x_1 + w_2 x_2 + \alpha = 0$ of the LDA decision boundary between classes 1 and 2.
  3. (c) Interpretation: Explain geometrically why the LDA boundary in part (b) need not be perpendicular to the line joining the two class means $\boldsymbol{\mu}_1$ and $\boldsymbol{\mu}_2$ (as it would be for $\Sigma = I$). What property of $\Sigma$ determines the angle?
  4. (d) Extension: With three classes, how many distinct pairwise LDA decision boundaries exist? Are all of them necessary for the multiclass rule $\hat{c} = \operatorname*{arg\,max}_c \tilde{\delta}_c(\mathbf{x})$? Explain.
Exercise 9.4 · Bias-Variance Analysis of QDA vs. LDA
Choosing Between QDA and LDA for Credit Risk Prediction

A bank wants to classify loan applicants as low risk ($C$) or high risk ($D$) using $d$ financial features. They have $n = 500$ total training examples with $n_C = n_D = 250$. The true data-generating distributions are $p(\mathbf{x}|C) = \mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{\mu}_C, \Sigma_C)$ and $p(\mathbf{x}|D) = \mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{\mu}_D, \Sigma_D)$ with $\Sigma_C \neq \Sigma_D$.

  1. (a) Derivation: Show that the Bayes-optimal error rate for this two-class Gaussian problem is $\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x}}[\min(P(C|\mathbf{x}), P(D|\mathbf{x}))]$ and explain why neither LDA nor QDA can achieve this rate with finite data.
  2. (b) Computation: For $d = 10$, count the total number of free parameters in (i) LDA and (ii) QDA. For $d = 50$, repeat. At what value of $d$ does QDA's parameter count exceed $n = 500$?
  3. (c) Interpretation: Even though $\Sigma_C \neq \Sigma_D$ (so QDA's model is "correct" and LDA's is "wrong"), argue that for small $n/d$ ratios, LDA might still achieve lower test error than QDA. What statistical phenomenon drives this?
  4. (d) Data Science Application: Propose a practical procedure (using validation data) to choose between LDA and QDA, and between using $d$ original features vs. reducing to $k < d$ principal components first. What is the computational cost of your procedure?
Exercise 9.5 · Asymmetric Loss and Posterior Calibration
Adjusting QDA for Cost-Sensitive Disease Screening

A hospital uses QDA to screen patients for a rare disease with prevalence $\pi_C = 0.01$ (disease) and $\pi_D = 0.99$ (healthy). The cost of a missed diagnosis (false negative) is $\lambda_{FN} = 1000$ (in arbitrary units) and the cost of an unnecessary follow-up (false positive) is $\lambda_{FP} = 10$.

  1. (a) Derivation: Derive the optimal decision threshold $p^*$ that minimizes expected cost, and express the optimal decision rule in terms of the QDA discriminant difference $\delta_C(\mathbf{x}) - \delta_D(\mathbf{x})$. What threshold $t^*$ replaces the default threshold of 0?
  2. (b) Computation: Given that QDA with equal priors and symmetric loss classifies a patient at the boundary (posterior 50%), recompute the posterior probability that this patient has the disease after accounting for (i) the true prior $\pi_C = 0.01$ and (ii) the asymmetric loss.
  3. (c) Interpretation: Sketch how the decision boundary changes geometrically in feature space as $\lambda_{FN}/\lambda_{FP}$ increases from 1 to $\infty$. What happens to the region of feature space classified as "disease" (class $C$)?
  4. (d) Extension: Suppose you want to guarantee that at most 5% of true disease patients are missed (false negative rate $\leq 0.05$). Express this constraint in terms of the posterior probability and determine the decision threshold. Does this threshold depend on $\lambda_{FP}$?
